blocks.text: Multiplying a vector by a matrix usually changes both its length and its direction. Eigenvalues are about the rare, special exception: certain vectors that a given matrix only stretches or shrinks, never redirects, and the eigenvalue is exactly the number describing how much that stretching or shrinking is.

blocks.alt: A matrix acting on vectors, where most vectors change direction but special vectors only get scaled by the eigenvalue
blocks.caption: This lesson is entirely about that scaling number.

blocks.text: 1. The Eigenvalue Equation

The defining relationship is written Mv = lambda * v. M is the matrix, v is a special vector called an eigenvector, covered in its own dedicated lesson next, and lambda, the Greek letter typically used here, is the eigenvalue, a single number.

What this equation says in plain language: multiplying v by the full matrix M produces the exact same result as just multiplying v by the single number lambda. The entire matrix collapses down to acting like a plain scalar, but only for this one special vector.

Only square matrices have eigenvalues at all, which fits the pattern already seen with inverses and determinants in this module, several of the deeper properties of a matrix only make sense once the matrix has the same number of rows as columns.

Lambda is a Greek letter, pronounced lam-duh, used throughout linear algebra and machine learning specifically to mean an eigenvalue or, in unrelated contexts, a regularization strength, so always check the surrounding context for which meaning is intended.
2. What Makes This Special

Take almost any ordinary vector and multiply it by a matrix, and the result typically points in a new direction entirely, not just a scaled version of the original. Eigenvectors are the exception: matrix M applied to an eigenvector produces a result pointing in exactly the same, or exactly the opposite, direction, only longer or shorter.

code.content:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 3]])
v = np.array([1, 0])
print(M.dot(v))   # [2 0], same direction as v, just scaled by 2

blocks.text: This special direction is called an eigenvector, and it is always paired with its own eigenvalue: the eigenvector names the direction, the eigenvalue names how much that direction gets stretched or shrunk.
2.1 A Non-Example, for Contrast

Trying a vector that is not an eigenvector of the same matrix shows the contrast clearly. Multiplying (1, 1) by the diagonal matrix above gives (2, 3), which points in a genuinely different direction than (1, 1) did, confirming it is not one of this matrix special directions.

code.content:
v = np.array([1, 1])
print(M.dot(v))   # [2 3], a different direction than (1, 1)

blocks.text: 3. Computing Eigenvalues in Code

code.content:
M = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 3]])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(M)
print(eigenvalues)   # [2. 3.]

blocks.text: For this particular matrix, a diagonal matrix, the eigenvalues turn out to be exactly the diagonal entries themselves, 2 and 3, which is always true for any diagonal matrix and makes it a good first example to build intuition from.

The function name eig returns eigenvalues and eigenvectors together as a pair, since libraries compute both from the same underlying numerical routine, it is rarely more expensive to ask for both than to ask for eigenvalues alone.
4. A Worked Example By Hand

Diagonal matrices make eigenvalues easy to verify without any real calculation. Multiplying (1, 0) by the matrix above scales it by exactly 2, and multiplying (0, 1) scales it by exactly 3, matching the two eigenvalues found above.

code.content:
v1 = np.array([1, 0])
v2 = np.array([0, 1])
print(M.dot(v1))   # [2 0] = 2 * v1
print(M.dot(v2))   # [0 3] = 3 * v2

blocks.text: 5. A Matrix Can Have Multiple Eigenvalues
An n by n matrix has up to n eigenvalues, one for each independent special scaling direction it contains. The 2 by 2 example above had exactly 2, a larger matrix can have correspondingly more.

Not every matrix has eigenvalues that are as easy to spot by inspection as a diagonal matrix does. Most real matrices need the actual eigenvalue-finding procedure a library implements, which involves solving a specific polynomial equation derived from the matrix, well beyond what is practical to do by hand past a 2 by 2 or 3 by 3 example.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A 3 by 3 identity matrix, from the identity matrix lesson, has the eigenvalue 1 repeated three times, once for every direction, since every vector is already an eigenvector of the identity matrix with eigenvalue 1. Repeated eigenvalues like this are common and perfectly valid, not a sign of an error.

blocks.text: 6. Negative and Zero Eigenvalues

An eigenvalue does not have to be positive. A negative eigenvalue means the matrix flips that special direction to point the opposite way while still only scaling it, no rotation to some other direction involved. An eigenvalue of exactly zero means the matrix collapses that entire direction down to nothing, a direct connection to the rank of a matrix lesson: a matrix with an eigenvalue of zero is not full rank, and cannot be inverted.

It is worth trying this zero-eigenvalue connection directly: any matrix already identified as singular in the matrix inverse lesson will always show at least one eigenvalue of exactly zero when checked, since the two ideas describe the exact same underlying fact from two different angles.

7. Why Eigenvalues Matter in AI

items: Principal component analysis, covered later in this module, ranks directions in data by the size of their eigenvalues, largest eigenvalue first.
Stability analysis: whether a repeated process grows, shrinks, or stays steady over time often comes down to whether relevant eigenvalues are above, below, or equal to 1.
Diagnosing a matrix invertibility instantly: a zero eigenvalue means the matrix is singular, covered in the matrix inverse lesson.

blocks.text: These uses share a common thread worth naming directly: eigenvalues are almost always used to rank or judge directions, biggest eigenvalue usually meaning most important, most dominant, or fastest growing, depending on the specific context they show up in.
8. Eigenvalues, the Determinant, and the Trace

Two quick sanity checks come from the determinant and the trace, the sum of the diagonal entries. The product of all of a matrix eigenvalues always equals its determinant, and the sum of all its eigenvalues always equals its trace, no matter how the matrix is arranged.

code.content:
M = np.array([[4, 1], [2, 3]])
eigenvalues, _ = np.linalg.eig(M)
print(eigenvalues)              # [5. 2.]
print(np.prod(eigenvalues))     # 10.0, matches det(M)
print(np.sum(eigenvalues))      # 7.0, matches trace(M) = 4 + 3

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: This gives a fast way to sanity check a hand computed or code computed eigenvalue list without recomputing anything from scratch: add up the diagonal, add up the eigenvalues you found, and confirm the two totals match. If they do not, an eigenvalue was miscalculated or missed.

blocks.text: 9. Where Eigenvalues Actually Come From

Eigenvalues are not guessed, they are the solutions to a specific equation called the characteristic equation, written det(M minus lambda times I) equals zero, where I is the identity matrix from the identity matrix lesson. Rearranging the eigenvalue equation Mv = lambda v into (M minus lambda I)v = 0 shows why: that equation only has a nonzero solution v when the matrix (M minus lambda I) is singular, which by the rank and inverse lessons means its determinant must be zero.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
M = sp.Matrix([[4, 1], [2, 3]])
lam = sp.symbols("lambda")
char_eq = (M - lam * sp.eye(2)).det()
print(sp.factor(char_eq))     # (lambda - 2) * (lambda - 5)
print(sp.solve(char_eq, lam)) # [2, 5]

blocks.text: This is the actual mechanical definition libraries use under the hood: solve the characteristic polynomial for lambda, then for each root, solve the now-singular system (M minus lambda I)v = 0 to find its matching eigenvector. Section 14 works through exactly this process by hand on a small matrix.

For anything larger than a 3 by 3 or 4 by 4 matrix, solving the characteristic polynomial by hand becomes impractical, which is why every real workflow calls a library routine instead, the characteristic polynomial explanation here exists to demystify what that routine is actually doing under the hood.
10. Eigenvalues of Symmetric Matrices

A symmetric matrix, one that equals its own transpose as covered in the matrix transpose lesson, always has real eigenvalues, never complex ones, and its eigenvectors can always be chosen to be mutually perpendicular. This is not true of matrices in general, where eigenvalues can come out as complex numbers with no straightforward geometric picture.

code.content:
S = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])          # symmetric: S == S.T
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(S)
print(eigenvalues)     # [3. 1.], both real
print(eigenvectors.T @ eigenvectors)   # close to the identity: eigenvectors are orthogonal

blocks.text: Covariance matrices, the matrices PCA operates on, are always symmetric by construction, which is precisely why PCA can always rely on getting clean, real, mutually perpendicular eigenvectors to use as new axes, with no messy complex number cases to special case around.
11. Eigenvalues and Repeated Matrix Multiplication

Applying a matrix to its own eigenvector repeatedly is equivalent to just raising its eigenvalue to that same power, since Mv = lambda v means M squared v = lambda squared v, M cubed v = lambda cubed v, and so on. This turns a repeated, expensive matrix multiplication into cheap ordinary exponentiation, as long as you are working along an eigenvector direction.

code.content:
M = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 0.5]])
v = np.array([1, 0])              # an eigenvector, eigenvalue 2
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(M, 10).dot(v))   # [1024, 0] = 2**10 times v

blocks.text: This single fact explains why some repeated processes blow up and others settle down. If every eigenvalue of a matrix has magnitude below 1, repeated application shrinks any vector toward zero. If any eigenvalue has magnitude above 1, repeated application eventually blows that direction up without bound. Training dynamics, iterative solvers, and recurrent neural network stability are all read directly off this same test.
12. A Zero Eigenvalue Means Singular

This connects directly back to the rank and inverse lessons: a matrix has at least one zero eigenvalue exactly when it is singular, meaning rank deficient and non invertible. A zero eigenvalue means there is some direction v for which Mv equals 0v, in other words a nonzero vector that the matrix collapses entirely to zero, which is exactly the null space idea from the rank lesson.

code.content:
M = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])     # the same rank deficient matrix from the rank lesson
print(np.linalg.eig(M)[0])          # [0. 5.], confirming a zero eigenvalue
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(M))     # 1, matching the fact that one direction collapses

blocks.text: 13. Eigenvalues in Covariance and PCA

Section 7 already flagged PCA as a major use case, and this section makes the connection concrete. Computing the covariance matrix of a dataset, then finding its eigenvalues, ranks every direction in the data by how much variance lies along it, largest eigenvalue first. The eigenvector attached to the largest eigenvalue is the single direction along which the data varies the most, exactly the first principal component.

code.content:
X = np.random.randn(200, 3) @ np.array([[3,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0.2]])
cov = np.cov(X.T)
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(cov)
print(np.sort(eigenvalues)[::-1])   # largest eigenvalue corresponds to the most spread out direction

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: If the three eigenvalues of a covariance matrix come out as roughly 9, 1, and 0.04, that says the first direction alone carries about 90 percent of the total variance, the second a small remainder, and the third is nearly flat and safe to drop. This is precisely how PCA decides how many dimensions to keep, a topic covered in full in the PCA intuition lesson later in this module.

blocks.text: This same ranking-by-eigenvalue idea extends beyond PCA to spectral clustering and graph based recommendation methods, wherever a symmetric matrix summarizing pairwise relationships needs to be reduced to its most informative few directions.

blocks.text: 15. Practice: Verify an Eigenvalue by Hand

Take the matrix [[5, 4], [1, 2]] and the claimed eigenvalue 6 with eigenvector (4, 1). Confirm the relationship by hand before checking with code: multiply the matrix by the vector, and confirm the result equals 6 times the original vector.

code.content:
M = np.array([[5, 4], [1, 2]])
v = np.array([4, 1])
print(M.dot(v))     # [24, 6]
print(6 * v)         # [24, 6], confirming the match

items: Multiplying M by v by hand reinforces the mechanics behind the eigenvalue equation from section 1.
Matching the result against 6 times v directly practices the definition of what makes a vector an eigenvector, first shown in section 2.

blocks.text: 16. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming every vector has an eigenvalue relationship with a given matrix, only the specific eigenvectors do.
Forgetting that a zero eigenvalue signals a singular, non-invertible matrix, directly connecting to the matrix inverse and rank lessons.
Confusing the eigenvalue, a single scaling number, with the eigenvector, the actual special direction it applies to, covered in the next lesson.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

Eigenvalues also give a fast diagnostic for whether a matrix is invertible, whether repeated application of a process explodes or settles down, and how much variance a given direction in a dataset actually carries.

An eigenvalue is the number lambda in Mv = lambda v, describing exactly how much a matrix stretches, shrinks, or flips one of its special directions, without changing that direction to something else entirely. An n by n matrix can have up to n such eigenvalues, and a zero eigenvalue is a direct signal that the matrix is singular.

This single number turns out to carry enormous weight elsewhere in AI, ranking the importance of directions in data for PCA, revealing whether a repeated process is stable, and offering an instant invertibility check, all reasons this lesson is worth understanding solidly before moving to eigenvectors themselves.

The eigenvectors lesson picks up immediately from here, covering the paired direction vectors that go alongside each eigenvalue, and the orthogonality, singular value decomposition, and PCA lessons ahead all build directly on the ideas introduced in this lesson.
